## SunShot Initiative Cost Goals

The SunShot cost goal for CSP is $0.06/kWh, which represents the overall target for making concentrating solar power cost competitive.

## Gen3 CSP Program Target

For more recent developments, the Gen3 CSP program targets an energy cost of $0.05/kWh. The project goal is to demonstrate CSP technology capable of reliable operation at costs less than $60/MWh.

## Molten Salt Thermal Storage Costs

Heat storage costs with molten salt technology range from 15 to 25 EUR/kWhth, while capital costs are listed at 25 EUR/kWhth stored in a molten salt tank. More specifically, the storage capacity for molten salt storage is 40 to 110 kWh/ton, which helps put costs into perspective relative to material requirements.

## Salt Pricing (2025)

**Potassium Nitrate (KNO3):**
The price of Potassium Nitrate in the United States reached 883 USD per metric ton in November 2025, while the average potassium nitrate price in China reached approximately USD 748.33 per metric ton on an FOB Shanghai basis during Q4 2025.

**Sodium Nitrate (NaNO3):**
The price of Sodium Nitrate in the United States increased to 1,070 USD per metric ton in November 2025, and sodium nitrate prices in Europe reached 1.21 USD/kg (approximately 1,210 USD/metric ton) in December 2025.

The actual cost of molten salt thermal storage depends on multiple factors including tank design, materials used for containment, and specific system configuration. By 2025, conventional stainless steel tank solutions became 11% more expensive than refractory concrete alternatives.

content.text:
## 1. Define the system and its physics

5 MWh of **sensible heat** in a two-tank solar-salt system (60% NaNO₃ / 40% KNO₃), the standard CSP-industry design: cold tank ≈290°C, hot tank ≈565°C, ΔT≈275°C, cp≈1.5 kJ/kg·K.

Energy density = cp·ΔT = 1.5 × 275 / 3600 ≈ **115 Wh/kg** (≈115 kWh/tonne — matches the industry-cited range of 40–110 kWh/tonne, so the physics checks out).

→ Salt mass needed: 5,000,000 Wh ÷ 115 Wh/kg ≈ **43 tonnes**, volume ≈23 m³ (molten density ~1,900 kg/m³), split across two tanks.

## 2. Bottom-up component cost (the actual Fermi build)

Current nitrate prices are elevated (KNO₃ ≈$880/t, NaNO₃ ≈$1,070/t in the US in late 2025) versus the ~$500–600/t historical bulk-contract figure often used in older studies. I'll use a blended ~$700/t.

| Component | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Salt (43 t) | ~$700/t | $30,000 |
| Tanks, hot+cold (alloy-lined hot tank, insulated) | fabricated pressure vessels, ~25 m³ each | $180,000 |
| Heat exchangers (charge + discharge, specialty alloy) | high-temp molten-salt duty | $350,000 |
| Molten-salt pumps (2 + spare) | cantilever/sump pumps for 565°C salt | $100,000 |
| Trace heating, freeze protection, insulation | salt freezes ~220°C | $60,000 |
| Instrumentation & controls | | $80,000 |
| Piping & valves (high-temp alloy) | | $110,000 |
| Civil/foundation/structural | | $70,000 |
| **Direct cost subtotal** | | **$980,000** |
| Installation labor | | $180,000 |
| EPC markup/engineering/contingency (~20%) | | $230,000 |
| **Total installed** | | **≈$1.39M** |

**→ $1,390,000 / 5,000 kWh ≈ $280/kWh installed.**

**Sanity check via scaling law:** published large-scale (≥GWh, CSP-plant) molten-salt TES runs ~$25–30/kWh-th (≈25 €/kWh cited), and DOE's SunShot target was <$15/kWh-th. Applying the standard "six-tenths rule" for process equipment (cost ∝ size^0.6, so $/unit ∝ size^–0.4) across a ~1,000x scale jump from 5 MWh to ~GWh gives a predicted ~16x reduction — landing almost exactly on $280/kWh → ~$18/kWh. That's a strong internal-consistency check: **the salt itself is nearly free; essentially all the $/kWh cost at small scale is fixed-cost overhead (tanks, HX, pumps, controls) that doesn't shrink proportionally with capacity.** At 5 MWh you're paying for a full set of balance-of-plant equipment to move a trivial amount of energy.

## 3. Amortize over life, to $/kWh delivered

Molten salt has no electrochemical degradation — life is set by thermal-cycling fatigue of tanks/HX and insulation, typically **25 years**, with no real cycle-count limit (unlike batteries).

CRF at 7%/25yr ≈ 8.6%/yr → annualized capital ≈ $120,000/yr; +2% O&M ≈ $28,000/yr → **≈$148,000/yr**.

At ~350 full cycles/yr (5 MWh/cycle) → 1.75 GWh-th/yr throughput. Two very different end uses:

- **Direct heat delivery** (industrial process heat, no reconversion — the Rondo Energy/Antora model), efficiency ~95%: **≈8.9¢/kWh-th delivered**
- **Re-electrified** via a steam/Rankine cycle (a true "Carnot battery"), round-trip efficiency ~40–45%: **≈19.8¢/kWh-e delivered**

## 4. Li-ion comparison, same 5 MWh scale

2025 small-commercial containerized Li-ion BESS runs **$280–580/kWh** installed (vs. $117–300/kWh for utility-scale systems >100 MWh — batteries get the same scale benefit, and prices fell ~31% in 2025 alone). Using $300/kWh central estimate, ~13-year life, 90% RTE, same 350 cycles/yr:

- Annualized capital+O&M ≈$202,500/yr ÷ 1.575 GWh/yr delivered ≈ **12.9¢/kWh-e delivered**

## Verdict

| Mode | $/kWh delivered |
|---|---|
| Li-ion BESS (5 MWh) | ~13¢/kWh-e |
| Molten salt → turbine → electricity | ~20¢/kWh-e |
| Molten salt → direct process heat | ~9¢/kWh-th |

**Not competitive as an electricity-arbitrage device at this scale.** The theoretical cost advantage of molten salt (media is ~20x cheaper per kWh than a lithium cell) is wiped out twice over at 5 MWh: once by fixed balance-of-plant costs that don't scale down (pumps, HX, controls — the same items a 500 MWh plant needs), and again by the ~45% Rankine-cycle penalty if you insist on turning the heat back into electrons. Li-ion, despite being the intrinsically more expensive medium, wins because it stores and returns *electricity directly* at 90%+ efficiency with no energy-conversion tax.

**Is competitive — likely superior — if the end use is heat, not electricity.** Skipping reconversion is the whole trick: it's why every commercial molten-salt/firebrick "heat battery" company (Rondo, Antora, Fourth Power) targets industrial process heat and steam, not grid arbitrage. There, the comparison to Li-ion is moot anyway — batteries can't deliver 300–1000°C heat without their own lossy conversion step.

**The scale threshold matters more than the chemistry.** The six-tenths-rule check above suggests molten salt only reaches genuinely low $/kWh (~$20-30) at GWh-class scale — roughly 200-1000x bigger than this 5 MWh case. Below that, you're paying for a full chemical-plant-grade BOP to store a rounding error's worth of energy.

- [Sodium Nitrate Prices (Intratec)](https://www.intratec.us/chemical-markets/sodium-nitrate-price)

## 1. Define the system and its physics

5 MWh of **sensible heat** in a two-tank solar-salt system (60% NaNO₃ / 40% KNO₃), the standard CSP-industry design: cold tank ≈290°C, hot tank ≈565°C, ΔT≈275°C, cp≈1.5 kJ/kg·K.

Energy density = cp·ΔT = 1.5 × 275 / 3600 ≈ **115 Wh/kg** (≈115 kWh/tonne — matches the industry-cited range of 40–110 kWh/tonne, so the physics checks out).

→ Salt mass needed: 5,000,000 Wh ÷ 115 Wh/kg ≈ **43 tonnes**, volume ≈23 m³ (molten density ~1,900 kg/m³), split across two tanks.

## 2. Bottom-up component cost (the actual Fermi build)

Current nitrate prices are elevated (KNO₃ ≈$880/t, NaNO₃ ≈$1,070/t in the US in late 2025) versus the ~$500–600/t historical bulk-contract figure often used in older studies. I'll use a blended ~$700/t.

| Component | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Salt (43 t) | ~$700/t | $30,000 |
| Tanks, hot+cold (alloy-lined hot tank, insulated) | fabricated pressure vessels, ~25 m³ each | $180,000 |
| Heat exchangers (charge + discharge, specialty alloy) | high-temp molten-salt duty | $350,000 |
| Molten-salt pumps (2 + spare) | cantilever/sump pumps for 565°C salt | $100,000 |
| Trace heating, freeze protection, insulation | salt freezes ~220°C | $60,000 |
| Instrumentation & controls | | $80,000 |
| Piping & valves (high-temp alloy) | | $110,000 |
| Civil/foundation/structural | | $70,000 |
| **Direct cost subtotal** | | **$980,000** |
| Installation labor | | $180,000 |
| EPC markup/engineering/contingency (~20%) | | $230,000 |
| **Total installed** | | **≈$1.39M** |

**→ $1,390,000 / 5,000 kWh ≈ $280/kWh installed.**

**Sanity check via scaling law:** published large-scale (≥GWh, CSP-plant) molten-salt TES runs ~$25–30/kWh-th (≈25 €/kWh cited), and DOE's SunShot target was <$15/kWh-th. Applying the standard "six-tenths rule" for process equipment (cost ∝ size^0.6, so $/unit ∝ size^–0.4) across a ~1,000x scale jump from 5 MWh to ~GWh gives a predicted ~16x reduction — landing almost exactly on $280/kWh → ~$18/kWh. That's a strong internal-consistency check: **the salt itself is nearly free; essentially all the $/kWh cost at small scale is fixed-cost overhead (tanks, HX, pumps, controls) that doesn't shrink proportionally with capacity.** At 5 MWh you're paying for a full set of balance-of-plant equipment to move a trivial amount of energy.

## 3. Amortize over life, to $/kWh delivered

Molten salt has no electrochemical degradation — life is set by thermal-cycling fatigue of tanks/HX and insulation, typically **25 years**, with no real cycle-count limit (unlike batteries).

CRF at 7%/25yr ≈ 8.6%/yr → annualized capital ≈ $120,000/yr; +2% O&M ≈ $28,000/yr → **≈$148,000/yr**.

At ~350 full cycles/yr (5 MWh/cycle) → 1.75 GWh-th/yr throughput. Two very different end uses:

- **Direct heat delivery** (industrial process heat, no reconversion — the Rondo Energy/Antora model), efficiency ~95%: **≈8.9¢/kWh-th delivered**
- **Re-electrified** via a steam/Rankine cycle (a true "Carnot battery"), round-trip efficiency ~40–45%: **≈19.8¢/kWh-e delivered**

## 4. Li-ion comparison, same 5 MWh scale

2025 small-commercial containerized Li-ion BESS runs **$280–580/kWh** installed (vs. $117–300/kWh for utility-scale systems >100 MWh — batteries get the same scale benefit, and prices fell ~31% in 2025 alone). Using $300/kWh central estimate, ~13-year life, 90% RTE, same 350 cycles/yr:

- Annualized capital+O&M ≈$202,500/yr ÷ 1.575 GWh/yr delivered ≈ **12.9¢/kWh-e delivered**

## Verdict

| Mode | $/kWh delivered |
|---|---|
| Li-ion BESS (5 MWh) | ~13¢/kWh-e |
| Molten salt → turbine → electricity | ~20¢/kWh-e |
| Molten salt → direct process heat | ~9¢/kWh-th |

**Not competitive as an electricity-arbitrage device at this scale.** The theoretical cost advantage of molten salt (media is ~20x cheaper per kWh than a lithium cell) is wiped out twice over at 5 MWh: once by fixed balance-of-plant costs that don't scale down (pumps, HX, controls — the same items a 500 MWh plant needs), and again by the ~45% Rankine-cycle penalty if you insist on turning the heat back into electrons. Li-ion, despite being the intrinsically more expensive medium, wins because it stores and returns *electricity directly* at 90%+ efficiency with no energy-conversion tax.

**Is competitive — likely superior — if the end use is heat, not electricity.** Skipping reconversion is the whole trick: it's why every commercial molten-salt/firebrick "heat battery" company (Rondo, Antora, Fourth Power) targets industrial process heat and steam, not grid arbitrage. There, the comparison to Li-ion is moot anyway — batteries can't deliver 300–1000°C heat without their own lossy conversion step.

**The scale threshold matters more than the chemistry.** The six-tenths-rule check above suggests molten salt only reaches genuinely low $/kWh (~$20-30) at GWh-class scale — roughly 200-1000x bigger than this 5 MWh case. Below that, you're paying for a full chemical-plant-grade BOP to store a rounding error's worth of energy.
